details:
**Vladimir and Estragon**
The two tramps who wait for Godot throughout Samuel Beckett's absurdist "tragicomedy in two acts," first performed in French as En attendant Godot in 1953. They call each other "Didi" and "Gogo," pass the time with arguments, routines, and talk of leaving, and are repeatedly reminded that they cannot go because "We're waiting for Godot." Godot never arrives.

**"Nothing to be done"**
The play's opening line and recurring refrain. It is first spoken by Estragon as he struggles and fails to pull off his boot. At the end of Act I he leaves his boots behind on the stage.

**Pozzo and Lucky**
A pompous master and his slave who pass by in each act. Pozzo drives Lucky with a rope tied around his neck, makes him carry heavy bags, and eats chicken and wine while Estragon gnaws the leftover bones. When Estragon tries to wipe Lucky's tears, Lucky kicks him in the shins. In Act II the rope is shorter, Pozzo has gone blind, and Lucky has gone mute. When Pozzo falls and answers to both "Abel" and "Cain," Estragon concludes "He's all humanity."

**Lucky's "Think!" speech**
When Pozzo commands "Think!" and Lucky's bowler hat is placed on his head (he can only think while wearing it), Lucky gives a long, unpunctuated monologue. It begins "Given the existence as uttered forth in the public works of Puncher and Wattmann of a personal God quaquaquaqua with white beard" and includes "divine aphasia," "Testew and Cunard," and the "Acacacacademy of Anthropopopometry." It ends in a struggle when the others tear off his hat, with Lucky's last words "tennis... the stones... so calm... Cunard... unfinished," after which Pozzo tramples the hat and says "There's an end to his thinking!"

**The tree**
The only set piece on stage; the setting is given as "A country road. A tree. Evening." The tree is bare in Act I but has a few leaves in Act II, and it is where Vladimir and Estragon agree to wait.

**Hanging themselves from the tree**
Vladimir and Estragon repeatedly consider suicide. Estragon is excited that hanging would give them an erection (from which mandrakes are said to grow). At the end of the play they test Estragon's belt (a cord holding up his trousers) as a rope, but it breaks and his trousers fall down, and they put off the hanging until tomorrow.

**The Boy**
A messenger from Godot who appears at the end of each act to announce that Mr. Godot "won't come this evening but surely tomorrow." He says he minds Godot's goats while his brother minds the sheep, and that Godot beats his brother but not him. In Act II he claims never to have seen Vladimir and Estragon before.

**Carrots, turnips, and radishes**
Food from Estragon's and Vladimir's pockets. Estragon asks for a carrot but is first handed a turnip, and they disagree about whether the carrot tastes better or worse the more you eat it. Later only turnips and radishes are left, and Estragon turns down a black radish because he only likes the pink ones.

**The two thieves**
Early in Act I, Vladimir discusses the two thieves crucified with Christ and why only one of the four Evangelists says one was saved, yet everyone believes that version; Estragon calls people "bloody ignorant apes." Estragon says he remembers only the colored maps of the Holy Land in the Bible, with the Dead Sea pale blue.

**Bowler hats**
All four main characters wear bowler hats. In Act II, Vladimir and Estragon do a vaudeville routine of rapidly swapping their own hats with the one Lucky left behind.

**Lucky's dance, "The Net"**
Pozzo says Lucky used to dance the farandole, the fling, the jig, and others. When ordered to dance, Lucky performs awkward movements that Pozzo calls "The Net," because he thinks he is caught in a net. Vladimir and Estragon suggest names such as "The Scapegoat's Agony" and "The Hard Stool."

**"A dog came in the kitchen"**
The round that Vladimir sings at the start of Act II, about a dog that steals a crust of bread and is beaten to death with a ladle by the cook. The song loops back on itself, and Vladimir struggles to remember the words.

**Vladimir's bladder trouble**
Vladimir has kidney or bladder problems and has to run offstage to urinate, which stops him from finishing a joke about an Englishman in a brothel; when Estragon starts it, he yells "Stop it!" Estragon tells him he stinks of garlic, which Vladimir says is good for the kidneys.

**"Yes, let's go." / They do not move.**
Both acts end with one character suggesting they leave, the other agreeing, and the stage direction "They do not move." The play has been described as one in which "nothing happens, twice."

**Production history**
Beckett tried to block a Dutch production with an all-female cast, objecting that "women don't have prostates," a reference to Vladimir's urinary trouble. Susan Sontag staged the play by candlelight in besieged Sarajevo in 1993.
